Learning Objectives

By the end of this lecture, you should be able to:

  • Represent an image as a feature vector, compare images with the L2 distance, and classify them with k-NN.
  • Choose a hyperparameter on validation data, and evaluate a classifier with accuracy and the confusion matrix.
  • Explain the limitations of k-NN on raw pixels.
  • Cluster data with k-means, and use it to segment an image by color.
  • Compute PCA, interpret its components and reconstructions, and use PCA coordinates as compact features.
  • Explain linear classifiers, the SVM margin, soft margins, kernels, and multi-class SVMs, and train an SVM with OpenCV.

Supervised Learning: KNN

An Image Is a Vector

  • A 28 × 28 gray image is 784 numbers. Stack its rows into one long vector \(\mathbf{x} = (x_1, x_2, \dots, x_{784})\).
  • Compare two images pixel by pixel:

\[ \bbox[border: 2px solid #c53030; padding: 2px 6px]{d(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}') = \sqrt{\sum_{j=1}^{784} \left(x_j - x'_j\right)^2}}\;\;{\color{#c53030}{\begin{array}{l}\textbf{L2}\\ \textbf{distance}\end{array}}} \]

  • \(x_j\), \(x'_j\): value of pixel \(j\) (0 to 255) in images \(\mathbf{x}\) and \(\mathbf{x}'\).
  • Small \(d\): similar images. Large \(d\): different images.
  • The sneaker is closest to the other sneaker (\(d\) = 1,714) and farthest from the trouser (\(d\) = 3,033).

Nearest Neighbors on FashionMNIST

  • Query (left column): a test image.
  • Neighbors: the 5 training images with the smallest L2 distance to the query, closest first.
  • Green frame: same class as the query. Red frame: a different class.
  • 46 of 50 neighbors have the query’s class.
  • Mistakes come from look-alike classes: the shirt query has neighbors labeled Pullover, T-shirt/top.
  • Simple idea: label a new image like its nearest training images.

k-Nearest Neighbors (k-NN)

k-Nearest Neighbors (k-NN)

Training: store all training images and their labels.

Prediction for a new image \(\mathbf{x}\):

  1. Compute the distance from \(\mathbf{x}\) to every training image.
  2. Find the \(k\) closest training images.
  3. Predict the most common label among them (majority vote).
  • 2D points stand in for images: each point is a vector with 2 numbers instead of 784.
  • \(k\) = 7: votes are 5 purple, 2 blue \(\rightarrow\) predict purple.
  • \(k\) = 1: the single nearest point is blue \(\rightarrow\) predict blue. The answer depends on \(k\).

Decision Boundaries Change with k

  • Decision boundary: where the predicted class changes. Each location is colored by its k-NN prediction.
  • Small \(k\): jagged boundary with islands around single points. It fits the noise (overfitting).
  • Large \(k\): smooth boundary, but the arms of the spiral get washed out (underfitting).
  • \(k\) is a hyperparameter: choose it on validation data, like the polynomial degree.

Choosing k on FashionMNIST

  • Split the 60,000 training images: 50,000 training + 10,000 validation. Keep the 10,000 test images aside.
  • Same recipe as choosing the polynomial degree: for each \(k\) = 1, …, 20, predict the validation images with k-NN and measure the accuracy.
  • Best: \(k\) = 6 (validation accuracy 85.5%).
  • Test accuracy with \(k\) = 6, measured once: 85.0%.
  • The curve is flat: every \(k\) from 1 to 20 is within 1.7 points of the best.

k-NN in Code

  • KNearest_create(): an empty k-NN model.
  • train(X, cv2.ml.ROW_SAMPLE, y): stores the data. X: one image per row (float32); y: the labels.
  • findNearest(X, k): k-NN prediction for each row of X. Returns the predicted labels, the labels of the k neighbors, and their distances.
  • On our data (\(k\) = 6): test accuracy 85.0%, about 1 ms per test image.
import cv2
import numpy as np

# X_tr: (50000, 784) float32, y_tr: labels 0-9
# X_te: (10000, 784) float32, y_te: labels 0-9
knn = cv2.ml.KNearest_create()
knn.train(X_tr, cv2.ml.ROW_SAMPLE,
          y_tr.astype(np.float32))

# best_k: chosen on the validation set
_, pred, neighbors, dist = knn.findNearest(
    X_te, k=best_k)
pred = pred.ravel().astype(int)
print("test accuracy:", np.mean(pred == y_te))

k-NN: Full Code

import gzip
from pathlib import Path

import cv2
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# 1. Data: FashionMNIST as 784-vectors. Split 50,000 training / 10,000 validation; 10,000 test.
data_dir = Path("assets/datasets/fashion_mnist")    # folder with the four .gz files

def read_idx(name, offset):
    with gzip.open(data_dir / name) as f:
        return np.frombuffer(f.read(), np.uint8, offset=offset)

X = read_idx("train-images-idx3-ubyte.gz", 16).reshape(-1, 784).astype(np.float32)
y = read_idx("train-labels-idx1-ubyte.gz", 8).astype(int)
X_te = read_idx("t10k-images-idx3-ubyte.gz", 16).reshape(-1, 784).astype(np.float32)
y_te = read_idx("t10k-labels-idx1-ubyte.gz", 8).astype(int)
X_tr, y_tr, X_val, y_val = X[:50000], y[:50000], X[50000:], y[50000:]

# 2. "Training": store the training images.
knn = cv2.ml.KNearest_create()
knn.train(X_tr, cv2.ml.ROW_SAMPLE, y_tr.astype(np.float32))

# 3. Choose k on the validation set. One search for the 20 nearest neighbors
#    (closest first), then a majority vote among the first k of them.
ks = range(1, 21)
_, _, neighbors, _ = knn.findNearest(X_val, k=max(ks))
neighbors = neighbors.astype(int)
val_acc = []
for k in ks:
    pred = np.array([np.bincount(row[:k], minlength=10).argmax() for row in neighbors])
    val_acc.append(np.mean(pred == y_val))
best_k = ks[int(np.argmax(val_acc))]
print(f"best k = {best_k}, validation accuracy = {max(val_acc):.3f}")

# 4. Test accuracy with the chosen k, once.
_, pred, _, _ = knn.findNearest(X_te, k=best_k)
pred = pred.ravel().astype(int)
print(f"test accuracy = {np.mean(pred == y_te):.3f}")

# 5. Confusion matrix: row = true class, column = predicted class.
confusion = np.zeros((10, 10), int)
np.add.at(confusion, (y_te, pred), 1)
print(confusion)

# 6. Plot the validation curve.
plt.plot(ks, val_acc, "s-")
plt.xlabel("k")
plt.ylabel("validation accuracy")
plt.show()

Accuracy and the Confusion Matrix

  • Confusion matrix: entry (row \(i\), column \(j\)) = number of test images of class \(i\) predicted as class \(j\).
  • Diagonal: correct predictions. Off the diagonal: mistakes, and which classes get mixed up.
  • \(\text{accuracy} = \dfrac{\text{sum of the diagonal}}{\text{sum of all entries}}\)
  • k-NN (\(k\) = 6): 8,502 / 10,000 correct = 85.0%.
  • Easiest: Sneaker (97% correct). Hardest: Shirt (54%), most often called T-shirt/top (207 times).

Limitations of k-NN

  • Slow prediction: compares each new image with all 50,000 training images (about 1 ms per image on a CPU).
  • Stores all the data: 50,000 × 784 values = 157 MB. More data: more memory and slower predictions.
  • Pixel distance is not semantic: a 2-pixel shift is invisible to us, but changes many pixels.
    • The shifted shirt is 2,472 away from the original, but a coat is only 660 away.
    • Shifting all test images by 2 pixels drops the accuracy from 85.0% to 67.0%.
  • Next: better features and better classifiers.

Unsupervised Learning: Clustering and PCA

k-Means Clustering

  • Unsupervised: points without labels. Goal: group them into \(k\) clusters of nearby points.
  • Each cluster has a center. Each point belongs to the nearest center.

k-Means

  1. Pick \(k\) starting centers (e.g., \(k\) random points).
  2. Assign: each point joins its nearest center.
  3. Update: move each center to the mean of its points.
  4. Repeat 2–3 until the assignments stop changing.
  • Right: 300 points, \(k\) = 4, a poor start (three starting centers come from the top-left blob). Done after 8 assign/update rounds.
  • \(k\) is a hyperparameter. The result depends on the start: run several times, keep the best.

Color Segmentation with k-Means

  • Each pixel is a point \((R, G, B)\) in 3D color space: 854 × 1280 = 1,093,120 points.
  • k-means with \(k\) = 4 finds 4 typical colors (the centers).
  • Replace each pixel by its center color: the image splits into regions of similar color.
  • No labels needed: the colors group by themselves.
  • Color only: pixels of the same color land in one cluster, even on different objects.

k-Means in Code

  • cv2.kmeans(data, K, bestLabels, criteria, attempts, flags):
    • data: one point per row (float32); here \(N\) × 3 colors.
    • K: the number of clusters \(k\).
    • bestLabels: starting labels (None: not given).
    • criteria: stop after 20 rounds, or when the centers move less than 1.0.
    • attempts: 5 runs from different starts; keep the most compact.
    • flags: the starting centers. KMEANS_PP_CENTERS: spread out (k-means++).
  • Returns compactness (sum of squared distances to the centers), labels (cluster of each point), centers (\(k\) × 3).
  • centers[labels]: each pixel → its center color.
import cv2
import numpy as np

image = cv2.imread("fruits.jpg")        # H x W x 3 (BGR)
pixels = image.reshape(-1, 3).astype(np.float32)

stop = cv2.TERM_CRITERIA_EPS + cv2.TERM_CRITERIA_MAX_ITER
criteria = (stop, 20, 1.0)   # 20 rounds or moves < 1.0
compactness, labels, centers = cv2.kmeans(
    pixels, 4, None, criteria, 5, cv2.KMEANS_PP_CENTERS)

segmented = centers[labels.ravel()].reshape(image.shape)
cv2.imwrite("fruits_k4.png", segmented.astype(np.uint8))

PCA: The Directions of Largest Variance

  • PCA (principal component analysis): find the directions in which the data varies the most.

PCA

  1. Subtract the mean from every point.
  2. First component \(\mathbf{u}_1\): the direction of largest variance.
  3. Next components \(\mathbf{u}_2, \mathbf{u}_3, \dots\): largest remaining variance, perpendicular to the previous ones.
  4. Keep the first \(k\). Describe each point by its \(k\) coordinates along them.
  • The components are the eigenvectors of the data’s covariance matrix.
  • Right: \(\mathbf{u}_1\) holds 93% of the variance. Keep only the coordinate along \(\mathbf{u}_1\): 1 number instead of 2, and the points barely move.

PCA on FashionMNIST

  • PCA of the 50,000 training images, each a vector of 784 numbers.
  • Mean image \(\boldsymbol{\mu}\) and components \(\mathbf{u}_j\) are 784-vectors too: show them as images.
  • Red: add ink to the mean. Blue: remove ink. Early components: coarse shapes. Later: finer details.
  • Variance kept: 72% with 10 components, 86% with 50. 187 of the 784 components keep 95%.

Reconstruction with k Components

  • Any image is the mean plus a weighted sum of components:

\[ \bbox[border: 2px solid #c53030; padding: 2px 6px]{\hat{\mathbf{x}} = \boldsymbol{\mu} + a_1 \mathbf{u}_1 + \dots + a_k \mathbf{u}_k}\;\;{\color{#c53030}{\begin{array}{l}\textbf{PCA}\\ \textbf{reconstruction}\end{array}}} \]

  • \(\boldsymbol{\mu}\): mean image; \(\mathbf{u}_j\): component \(j\).
  • \(a_j = \mathbf{u}_j \cdot (\mathbf{x} - \boldsymbol{\mu})\): coordinate of image \(\mathbf{x}\) along \(\mathbf{u}_j\).
  • With \(k\) = 50 numbers instead of 784, the garment is still easy to recognize.
  • So the coordinates \((a_1, \dots, a_k)\) are compact features: an input for a classifier.

PCA Features for Recognition

  • Left: PCA uses no labels, yet with 2 numbers per image many classes form their own regions; look-alike classes overlap.
  • Right: 20 features: within 1 point of the 784 pixels (84.4% vs. 85.0%). From 50 on, slightly better (the small components are mostly pixel noise).
  • Still pixel-based: a 2-pixel shift drops k-NN on 50 PCA features to 66.0%.

PCA in Code

  • PCACompute(data, mean, maxComponents): data has one image per row. mean=None: compute the mean. Returns the mean \(\boldsymbol{\mu}\) (1 × 784) and the components \(\mathbf{u}_j\) (one per row: 50 × 784).
  • PCAProject(X, mean, vecs): the coordinates \(a_1, \dots, a_k\) of each row of X.
  • PCABackProject(A, mean, vecs): the reconstructions \(\boldsymbol{\mu} + a_1 \mathbf{u}_1 + \dots + a_k \mathbf{u}_k\).
  • k-NN on PCA features (\(k\) = 6 neighbors, test set):
Input Numbers Accuracy Time / image
pixels 784 85.0% 1.2 ms
PCA 50 85.6% 0.1 ms
  • About the same accuracy, 15× faster, 16× less memory.
  • Next: a better classifier on the same features.
import cv2
import numpy as np

# X_tr: (50000, 784), X_te: (10000, 784) float32
mu, U = cv2.PCACompute(X_tr, mean=None, maxComponents=50)
F_tr = cv2.PCAProject(X_tr, mu, U)     # (50000, 50)
F_te = cv2.PCAProject(X_te, mu, U)     # (10000, 50)

X_hat = cv2.PCABackProject(F_te, mu, U)    # (10000, 784)
print("MSE:", np.mean((X_hat - X_te) ** 2))

# Any classifier can use the features, e.g., k-NN:
knn = cv2.ml.KNearest_create()
knn.train(F_tr, cv2.ml.ROW_SAMPLE, y_tr.astype(np.float32))
_, pred, _, _ = knn.findNearest(F_te, k=best_k)

Supervised Learning: SVM

Linear Classifiers

  • A linear classifier scores an input with a weighted sum:

\[ \bbox[border: 2px solid #c53030; padding: 2px 6px]{f(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{w} \cdot \mathbf{x} + b}\;\;{\color{#c53030}{\begin{array}{l}\textbf{linear}\\ \textbf{classifier}\end{array}}} \]

  • \(\mathbf{x}\): input (2 numbers here; 50 PCA features for an image). \(\mathbf{w}\): weights; \(b\): bias. Both learned.
  • Predict orange if \(f(\mathbf{x}) > 0\), blue otherwise. The decision boundary \(f(\mathbf{x}) = 0\) is a line (a “hyperplane” in more dimensions).
  • Lines A, B, C all separate the 60 training points. Which one is best?
  • On 1,000 new points, line C makes the fewest mistakes. It stays far from both classes.

The SVM Margin

  • Margin: the distance from the boundary to the closest training points.
  • SVM (support vector machine): the linear classifier with the largest margin (line C before). A wide gap is safer for new points.
  • Support vectors: the points on or inside the margin. They alone fix the boundary; moving any other point changes nothing.
  • Overlapping classes: some points must be inside the margin or on the wrong side (soft margin).
  • Hyperparameter \(C\): the penalty for those points.
    • Small \(C\): wide margin, many points inside.
    • Large \(C\): narrow margin, fewer points inside.

Kernel SVM: Nonlinear Boundaries

  • Middle: a new feature \(z = x_1^2 + x_2^2\) makes the classes separable by a plane. Back in 2D, the plane becomes a circle.
  • A kernel does this without computing the new features: it only needs a similarity between two points. RBF kernel \(K(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}') = e^{-\gamma \|\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}'\|^2}\): near 1 for close points, near 0 for far ones.
  • \(\gamma\): how far each training point’s influence reaches. Like \(C\), choose it on validation data.

Multi-Class SVM: One vs. Rest

One vs. Rest

  1. For each class \(c\): train a binary SVM, class \(c\) (+1) vs. all other classes (−1).
  2. New image: compute all class scores \(f_c(\mathbf{x})\).
  3. Predict the class with the highest score.
  • 10 FashionMNIST classes: 10 binary SVMs.
  • OpenCV’s SVM handles multiple classes by itself, with one vs. one: one SVM per pair of classes, 45 SVMs for 10 classes, then a majority vote.

SVM in Code

  • setType(SVM_C_SVC): classification with a soft margin.
  • setKernel(SVM_RBF), setC(...), setGamma(...): kernel and hyperparameters.
  • train(F, ROW_SAMPLE, y): F one feature vector per row (float32); y labels (int32).
  • predict(F): predicted labels.
  • Choose \(C\) and \(\gamma\) on the validation set (training on 10,000 images to save time). Validation accuracy:
\(\gamma\) = 0.01 \(\gamma\) = 0.03 \(\gamma\) = 0.1
\(C\) = 1 84.3% 85.8% 86.1%
\(C\) = 10 86.4% 86.9% 86.3%
\(C\) = 100 86.7% 85.9% 86.2%
  • Final model on all 50,000 training images: test accuracy 88.9%, trained in 11 s.
import cv2
import numpy as np

# F_tr, F_te: PCA features (50 per image), scaled
svm = cv2.ml.SVM_create()
svm.setType(cv2.ml.SVM_C_SVC)
svm.setKernel(cv2.ml.SVM_RBF)
svm.setC(best_C)          # chosen on validation data
svm.setGamma(best_gamma)
svm.train(F_tr, cv2.ml.ROW_SAMPLE, y_tr.astype(np.int32))

_, pred = svm.predict(F_te)
print("test accuracy:", np.mean(pred.ravel() == y_te))

PCA + SVM: Full Code

import gzip
import time
from pathlib import Path

import cv2
import numpy as np

# 1. Data: FashionMNIST as 784-vectors. Split 50,000 training / 10,000 validation; 10,000 test.
data_dir = Path("assets/datasets/fashion_mnist")    # folder with the four .gz files

def read_idx(name, offset):
    with gzip.open(data_dir / name) as f:
        return np.frombuffer(f.read(), np.uint8, offset=offset)

X = read_idx("train-images-idx3-ubyte.gz", 16).reshape(-1, 784).astype(np.float32)
y = read_idx("train-labels-idx1-ubyte.gz", 8).astype(np.int32)
X_te = read_idx("t10k-images-idx3-ubyte.gz", 16).reshape(-1, 784).astype(np.float32)
y_te = read_idx("t10k-labels-idx1-ubyte.gz", 8).astype(np.int32)
X_tr, y_tr, X_val, y_val = X[:50000], y[:50000], X[50000:], y[50000:]

# 2. PCA features (learned on the training set only), scaled to unit spread.
mu, U = cv2.PCACompute(X_tr, mean=None, maxComponents=50)
F_tr = cv2.PCAProject(X_tr, mu, U)
scale = F_tr.std()
F_tr = F_tr / scale
F_val = cv2.PCAProject(X_val, mu, U) / scale
F_te = cv2.PCAProject(X_te, mu, U) / scale

def train_svm(F, y, C, gamma):
    svm = cv2.ml.SVM_create()
    svm.setType(cv2.ml.SVM_C_SVC)
    svm.setKernel(cv2.ml.SVM_RBF)
    svm.setC(C)
    svm.setGamma(gamma)
    svm.setTermCriteria((cv2.TERM_CRITERIA_MAX_ITER + cv2.TERM_CRITERIA_EPS, 10000, 1e-3))
    svm.train(F, cv2.ml.ROW_SAMPLE, y)
    return svm

def accuracy(svm, F, y):
    return np.mean(svm.predict(F)[1].ravel() == y)

# 3. Choose C and gamma on the validation set (train on 10,000 images to save time).
best_acc, best_C, best_gamma = 0, None, None
for C in [1, 10, 100]:
    for gamma in [0.01, 0.03, 0.1]:
        acc = accuracy(train_svm(F_tr[:10000], y_tr[:10000], C, gamma), F_val, y_val)
        print(f"C = {C}, gamma = {gamma}: validation accuracy = {acc:.3f}")
        if acc > best_acc:
            best_acc, best_C, best_gamma = acc, C, gamma

# 4. Final model on all training images; test accuracy, once.
t0 = time.perf_counter()
svm = train_svm(F_tr, y_tr, best_C, best_gamma)
print(f"trained in {time.perf_counter() - t0:.0f} s")
print(f"C = {best_C}, gamma = {best_gamma}: test accuracy = {accuracy(svm, F_te, y_te):.3f}")

Our FashionMNIST Benchmark

Method Input Test accuracy Training time Time per image Model size
k-NN (\(k\) = 6) 784 pixels 85.0% none 1.2 ms 157 MB
k-NN (\(k\) = 6) 50 PCA features 85.6% PCA only 0.1 ms 10 MB
SVM (RBF) 50 PCA features 88.9% 11 s 0.04 ms 3.1 MB
  • SVM (\(C\) = 10, \(\gamma\) = 0.03): best so far, +3.9 points over k-NN on pixels, 32× faster per image. It keeps only 15,738 support vectors.
  • All three methods use pixel-based features. Neural networks learn their own features; we will compare them later.

Key Takeaways

  • An image is a vector of pixel values; the L2 distance compares two images pixel by pixel.
  • k-NN predicts the majority label of the \(k\) nearest training images. Small \(k\) overfits, large \(k\) underfits: choose \(k\) on validation data. The confusion matrix shows which classes get mixed up.
  • k-NN on pixels is slow and stores all the data, and pixel distance is not semantic: a 2-pixel shift can move an image farther than an image of another class.
  • k-means groups unlabeled points into \(k\) clusters by alternating assign and update. On pixel colors, it segments an image by color.
  • PCA finds the directions of largest variance. A few coordinates keep most of an image, so they make compact features: as accurate as pixels for k-NN, and much faster.
  • A linear classifier scores \(\mathbf{w} \cdot \mathbf{x} + b\). The SVM picks the boundary with the largest margin, set by the support vectors. \(C\) trades margin width for training mistakes; kernels (RBF, \(\gamma\)) give nonlinear boundaries.
  • On FashionMNIST, an SVM on PCA features beats k-NN, but all these methods still use pixel-based features.
